// question: 1
::P1Q1 Counting with a comparison::[html]<p>Five students sat an OSCE station and scored 78, 70, 91, 55 and 83.</p><pre><code>osce &lt;- c(78, 70, 91, 55, 83)<br><br>sum(osce &gt;\= 70)</code></pre><p>What does the second line print?</p>{
=[html]<p><code>4</code></p>#[html]<p>Correct, 78, 70, 91 and 83 are all 70 or above.</p>
~[html]<p><code>3</code></p>#[html]<p>That is the answer to <code>sum(osce &gt; 70)</code>, which drops the student who scored exactly 70. <code>&gt;\=</code> means "greater than <em>or equal to</em>", so that student is counted and the answer is 4.</p>
~[html]<p><code>5</code></p>#[html]<p>That is how many students there are, which is <code>length(osce)</code>. Only four of them reached 70; the student who scored 55 did not.</p>
~[html]<p><code>377</code></p>#[html]<p>That is the total of the five marks, <code>sum(osce)</code>. Here <code>sum()</code> is being given the <em>comparison</em>, not the marks, so it adds up TRUEs rather than scores.</p>
####[html]<p><code>4</code>. The comparison gives one <code>TRUE</code> or <code>FALSE</code> per student, and <code>sum()</code> counts each <code>TRUE</code> as 1. The bar matters\: <code>&gt;\=</code> keeps the student who scored exactly 70; <code>&gt;</code> drops them. Whenever a threshold is "70 or above", "at least 40" or "under 5", that single character decides whether a real person is counted.</p>
}

// question: 2
::P1Q2 Type coercion has consequences::[html]<p>You combine three values and R prints this\:</p><pre><code>c(1, 2, "three")<br>\#&gt; [1] "1"     "2"     "three"</code></pre><p>Those quotation marks around <code>1</code> and <code>2</code> matter. What can you no longer do?</p>{
=[html]<p>Anything arithmetic, all three values are now text, so <code>mean()</code> will not work</p>#[html]<p>Correct. One piece of text converted the whole vector.</p>
~[html]<p>Nothing, R remembers which two were numbers</p>#[html]<p>It does not. There is no mixed state\: the vector is entirely text now, and <code>"1"</code> is a character that happens to look like a number.</p>
~[html]<p>You can still average the first two, just not the third</p>#[html]<p>No. A vector is all one type by definition, so there are no longer any numbers in it to average. You would have to convert with <code>as.numeric()</code> first, and then decide what to do about <code>"three"</code>.</p>
~[html]<p>You can no longer print it, R errors on mixed types</p>#[html]<p>The opposite of the problem. R never errors here; it converts quietly and prints something that looks nearly right, which is exactly why this catches people out.</p>
####[html]<p>A vector holds one type only. Mix them and everything is silently converted to the most permissive type, which is text, so the numbers stop behaving like numbers. In real data this happens when one cell in a column holds "NA", "-", "&lt;1" or a stray space, and it is why <code>glimpse()</code> showing <code>&lt;chr&gt;</code> where you expected <code>&lt;dbl&gt;</code> is worth a second look.</p>
}

// question: 3
::P1Q3 What a comparison returns::[html]<p><code>scores</code> holds five marks. What does this line give you?</p><pre><code>scores &gt; 70</code></pre>{
=[html]<p>A vector of five <code>TRUE</code>/<code>FALSE</code> values, one per mark</p>#[html]<p>Correct, and that is the building block of everything you will do with <code>filter()</code> on Day 1.</p>
~[html]<p>A single <code>TRUE</code> or <code>FALSE</code> for the vector as a whole</p>#[html]<p>No. The comparison is applied element by element, so you get one answer per mark. Collapsing five answers into one takes a further step\: <code>any()</code>, <code>all()</code> or <code>sum()</code>.</p>
~[html]<p>The marks that are above 70</p>#[html]<p>Not by itself, though you are one step away\: <code>scores[scores &gt; 70]</code> uses those TRUEs and FALSEs to pull out the values. The comparison alone returns the TRUEs and FALSEs, not the marks.</p>
~[html]<p>The number of marks above 70</p>#[html]<p>That is <code>sum(scores &gt; 70)</code>. The comparison produces the TRUEs and FALSEs; <code>sum()</code> is what turns them into a count.</p>
####[html]<p>Five <code>TRUE</code>/<code>FALSE</code> values, one per element. R applies the comparison to the whole vector at once, which is why you never need a loop to ask a question of every row. That vector is what <code>sum()</code> counts and what <code>filter()</code> uses to decide which rows to keep.</p>
}

// question: 4
::P1Q4 Named arguments::[html]<p>What does this print?</p><pre><code>round(3.14159, digits \= 2)</code></pre>{
=[html]<p><code>3.14</code></p>#[html]<p>Correct, two decimal places.</p>
~[html]<p><code>3.142</code></p>#[html]<p>That is <code>digits \= 3</code>. The argument counts decimal places, not significant figures, for significant figures you want <code>signif()</code>.</p>
~[html]<p><code>3</code></p>#[html]<p>That is <code>round(3.14159)</code>, with no <code>digits</code> at all; the default is zero decimal places.</p>
~[html]<p><code>2</code></p>#[html]<p>No, <code>digits \= 2</code> is an instruction about <em>how</em> to round, not the value returned. The function still hands back a rounded version of 3.14159.</p>
####[html]<p><code>3.14</code>. A function takes its arguments in brackets, separated by commas, and naming them (<code>digits \= 2</code> rather than just <code>2</code>) makes the line readable to somebody who does not remember the argument order. Prefer named arguments; your reader, including future you, will not have the help page open.</p>
}
